item.title: Performance
item.description:
Two figures, each saved as PNG and as SVG, at matplotlib’s default size (6.4 x 4.8 in, 100 dpi):

  • line: Plot of a 1,000,000-point random walk;
  • imshow: Imshow of a 1000 x 1000 array (sin(i/37)·cos(j/23)), viridis.

Results

case go-plot median (s) matplotlib median (s) matplotlib / go-plot go-plot bytes matplotlib bytes
line, 1e6 points, PNG 0.055 0.065 1.2x 40,600 28,055
line, 1e6 points, SVG 0.019 0.053 2.8x 218,801 224,082
imshow 1000², PNG 0.025 0.042 1.7x 154,860 157,539
imshow 1000², SVG 0.020 0.042 2.1x 207,581 198,367

Spread (min / max over the 9 runs):

case go-plot matplotlib
line PNG 0.052 / 0.085 0.061 / 0.107
line SVG 0.018 / 0.024 0.050 / 0.063
imshow PNG 0.023 / 0.034 0.040 / 0.058
imshow SVG 0.019 / 0.034 0.041 / 0.049

go-plot’s PNGs are larger because it encodes with png.BestSpeed; matplotlib uses zlib’s default level.

Method

tools/compare/perf.py (driving tools/compare/perf/main.go):

  • both sides build the same data, with the same generator, before the clock starts; the clock covers creating the figure, plotting, and writing the file to memory;
  • every measurement is a fresh process on both sides (so neither keeps a warm glyph or path cache the other lacks), and the two are interleaved case by case, run by run, so that load changes on the host hit both alike;
  • 9 runs per case; the tables give medians, with the spread.

What is not in the numbers: Python’s interpreter start and import matplotlib.pyplot (about half a second on this machine), and the Go process start (a few milliseconds). A notebook keeps both warm, so the in-process time is the comparable one.

Host: Apple M4 Max, 16 cores, macOS; Go 1.27.2; Python 3.12.12, matplotlib 3.11.2, NumPy 2.5.3, Agg backend. The host was shared and loaded: load average 22.6 before the run and 21.7 after it, on 16 cores. Absolute times are therefore pessimistic for both; the interleaving is what keeps the ratio fair. Measured 2026-10-10.

Where the time goes, and what changed to get here

The first measurement of the line PNG was 0.124 s, half matplotlib’s speed. Profiling (go test -bench -cpuprofile) showed three costs, each now fixed:

  1. the data limits of the million points were recomputed per axis per draw (0.67 s of 2.2 s sampled): they are now taken once, when the artist is added;
  2. the coverage sweep of go-gfx’s rasteriser sorts each scanline’s crossings by insertion, quadratic in the crossings, and a dense polyline has thousands per scanline: strokes of more than 512 segments are now rasterised in 512-segment pieces (matplotlib has the same knob, agg.path.chunksize, off by default), whose seams are round joins, so the only visible change is that the line’s own two ends are round rather than projecting;
  3. STIX Two Math (for TeX labels) was parsed on every figure: it is now parsed only when a label contains TeX.

Like matplotlib, go-plot simplifies dense lines before drawing them (matplotlib’s PathSimplifier, ported): the 1e6-point walk is drawn as 11,738 vertices. That is why the SVG of a million points is about 220 kB on both sides.

Reproduce 

git clone https://github.com/go-plot/plot && cd plot/tools/compare
uv run --with matplotlib --with numpy python perf.py 9
